leads.name: Kauri Pine (City Botanic Gardens)

location.neighbourhood: City Botanic Gardens, south east of the formal flower garden

leads.why_not_verified: National Trust database only (Alice_Street_5): planted 1980, only roughly 45 years old. Too young to be a strong ancient-tree candidate; parked rather than pursued.

leads.name: Anzac (Turkish) Pines (City Botanic Gardens)

location.neighbourhood: City Botanic Gardens, eastern side near the George Street / Parliament House entrance

leads.why_not_verified: Planted 26 April 1979 from seed brought back from Lone Pine, Gallipoli, by veteran soldiers; historically significant (Anzac commemoration) but a group of 5 trees (2 originals plus 3 later replacements after 2 died), each only roughly 46 years old and modest (8m tall). Not pursued this pass: unclear whether it passes the single-collectible-point test given it is a small planted group with a mixed-age replacement history, and the age/size are both slight. Worth a judgement call by a future pass rather than a default no.

leads.name: The Bunya Tree of Manly West

location.neighbourhood: Road Reserve, Manly Road, Manly West (adjacent to 29 Whatmore Place)

leads.why_not_verified: Genuinely a single collectible point (unlike the blocked Bunya Pine Avenue): planted 1891 by John Hargreaves at the entrance to his farm and canning factory, the only one of the original planting still standing (recorded as 'approximately 110 years old' when documented, so roughly 135 now), individually listed on the Brisbane Heritage Register (heritage.brisbane.qld.gov.au/heritage-places/1024, local heritage place since 2004, citation Nov 2005) with tree-level coordinates. Source is directly fetched and solid (one official register), but this pass found no independent second source (searches surfaced only the same heritage citation, Wikipedia's Manly West and Queensland Places pages on the suburb generally, and the Hargreaves Factory history page at mappingbrisbanehistory.com.au, none of which was checked/fetched this pass, plus a draft citation PDF for a different nearby property). The bigger open question is distance: Manly West is roughly 14km from the CBD and about 35-43 minutes from Central by train per Translink/rome2rio, which is outside BRIEF_RESEARCH's ~30-minute day-trip guideline. Recorded as a lead rather than delivered: needs either a second source or a judgement call on whether it is close enough to include labeled honestly with its real travel time, same as Blarney-for-Cork or Fota-for-Cork precedents elsewhere on the site.

leads.name: The Hoop Pine of Ann Hill's Grave (Toowong Cemetery)

location.neighbourhood: Toowong Cemetery (Brisbane General Cemetery), near the grave of Ann Hill, section/grave number not yet found

leads.why_not_verified: Story only, not yet independently confirmed or pinned. Walter Hill, founding superintendent of Brisbane's City Botanic Gardens (the source of most of the city's other published trees), planted a hoop pine beside the grave of his daughter Ann Hill, who died in 1871 aged 21 and was the second person buried at Toowong Cemetery; 'today it is enormous' per a Queensland Stories blog post (roseobrienwriter.blog/2020/07/19/the-first-jacaranda/, found via WebSearch summary only, the live page 403s to WebFetch so this has not been independently read). No exact grave location, no measurements, and no second source found this pass. Toowong Cemetery (Queensland's largest, established 1866, itself on the Queensland Heritage Register id 601773) is a genuinely interesting second Brisbane cluster to research properly in a future pass, given Walter Hill's direct link to the already-published City Botanic Gardens trees, but this lead needs a proper research budget of its own rather than the tail end of a deepen pass.

blocked.name: Weeping Fig Avenue (City Botanic Gardens, eastern river path)

location.neighbourhood: City Botanic Gardens, eastern river path from the Edward Street entrance

blocked.reason: National Trust database (Alice_Street_13) explicitly describes this as an 'Avenue' of 9 trees planted by head gardener James Pink (1881-1886) along the riverbank, distinct from the already-published pair at the Alice Street gate (bne_009, a different National Trust entry, 147_Alice_Street_6). Not a single collectible point, same reasoning as the already-blocked Bunya Pine Avenue; never ship as one entry.

blocked.name: Bunya Pine Avenue (City Botanic Gardens)
blocked.reason: Not a single collectible point. Row of roughly 18 mature Bunya Pines planted by Walter Hill 1858-1867, skirting several hundred metres of the eastern river walk from inside the Edward Street entrance. Well documented (National Trust database: trusttrees.org.au/tree/QLD/Brisbane/Brisbane_City_Botanic_Gardens_Alice_Street_8; State Library of Queensland blog; Wikipedia calls it explicitly 'an avenue of bunya pines') but per the verify-pass rule an avenue is blocked regardless of fame or documentation quality. If a single standout specimen within the row is ever individually distinguished by a source (e.g. the largest or first-planted), it could be lifted out as its own entry.

blocked.name: Kelvin Grove Fig Trees and Air Raid Shelter
blocked.species: Weeping Fig (Ficus benjamina) and Hill's Fig (Ficus microcarpa var. hillii)

location.neighbourhood: Kelvin Grove Road, Kelvin Grove (Normanby Fiveways, Marshall Park, Prospect Terrace)

blocked.reason: Queensland Heritage Register listed (176 Kelvin Grove Road, designated 31 May 2005) but explicitly three separate groupings totalling about 15 trees (5 weeping figs at Normanby, 7 Hill's figs at Marshall Park, 3 weeping figs at Prospect Terrace) strung along roughly 1km of Kelvin Grove Road, planted in the early 20th century beautification era. Not a single collectible point, same reasoning as the already-blocked Bunya Pine Avenue and Weeping Fig Avenue; never ship as one entry. If a single standout specimen within one of the three groupings is ever individually distinguished by a source, it could be lifted out as its own entry.

note:
Brisbane City Council's 558-record significant/landscape tree overlay (data/registers/brisbane-significant-landscape-trees.json) carries NO species, name, age or vitality field, only a designation polygon centroid; it does not by itself clear the two-source bar for any tree and none of it was directly usable this pass without a named tree to match it to. Checked distance from each of the 8 verified City Botanic Gardens/Eagle Street trees to the nearest of the 558 overlay points: nearest was 520m (Eagle Street Fig Trees) and 535-745m for the Botanic Gardens trees, i.e. none of the overlay's individually-designated points sit close enough to plausibly be the same tree, so the overlay was not cited as a source for any of the 8. A future pass with more time could try to match named significant trees elsewhere in Brisbane (New Farm Park, Roma Street Parkland, Mount Coot-tha Botanic Gardens, university campuses) against the overlay's remaining ~550 unmatched points to grow a second cluster; this pass stayed inside the single City Botanic Gardens / Eagle Street cluster (max pairwise distance 1.12km) per the brief's preference for a dense walkable cluster over scattered candidates.

The Black Bean's 1951 Speaker's Chair anecdote (flagged in the original lead as worth confirming) does NOT hold for this specific tree: it was only about 7 years old in 1951, per its own recorded ~1944 planting date, so it could not have supplied the carving timber; National Trust's text describes the species/historical gift generally, not this specimen.
